articles.title: Japan economy shrinks 0.1% in Q3, first fall in 4 quarters as inflation hits households
articles.desc: The pushback from economists matters more for markets than the headline miss. If weak consumption is read as a sign of inflation rather than a reason to pause, December hike pricing should hold. That limits any lasting yen weakness from the data, although USD/JPY near 160 remains in intervention ter
articles.content: The pushback from economists matters more for markets than the headline miss. If weak consumption is read as a sign of inflation rather than a reason to pause, December hike pricing should hold. That limits any lasting yen weakness from the data, although USD/JPY near 160 remains in intervention territory. The risk lies in the board split some economists flagged. Further soft consumption data could give the doves more influence and push hike timing back, which would weigh on the yen and lift JGBs. Oil is the link in the middle. Energy-driven inflation is both hurting households and pushing the BOJ to tighten, so higher crude makes the policy dilemma worse. --- Earlier: Japan Q3 GDP shrinks 0.1% annualised vs +0.3% expected as exports and consumers weigh Recapping now. --- Japan’s shoppers are buckling under inflation, but rather than giving the BOJ a reason to pause, the squeeze on households is being read as further proof that rates need to keep rising. Summary: Japan’s GDP fell an annualised 0.1% in Q3, against a forecast of +0.3% growth and an upwardly revised +1.7% in Q2. It was the first fall in four quarters. Private consumption fell 0.3% as high prices, bad weather and fading tax-related demand weighed. Net exports cut 0.6 percentage point as energy imports recovered. Capex rose 1.6%, ahead of forecasts, helped by AI and labour-saving investment. The economy minister expects a gradual recovery but flagged Middle East risks. Economists see the BOJ’s tightening path intact, with a December hike possible, though some warned of a widening board split. Japan’s economy unexpectedly contracted in the July to September quarter as rising living costs forced households to cut back on spending. Economists say the weakness is unlikely to knock the Bank of Japan off its tightening path, Reuters reported. Gross domestic product fell an annualised 0.1%, against a median forecast of 0.3% growth, following an upwardly revised 1.7% expansion in the previous quarter. It was the first contraction in four quarters. On a quarterly basis, output slipped 0.02%, versus expectations of a 0.1% rise. Households did most of the damage. Private consumption, which makes up more than half of economic output, fell 0.3%, slightly worse than the expected 0.2% drop. Persistent inflation, heavy rain and typhoons weighed on spending. Purchases of cars and air conditioners also fell back after a temporary boost from tax and regulatory changes in the prior quarter. Economists warned that higher prices linked to Middle East tensions will keep squeezing households’ purchasing power, even as wages rise. Trade also took away from growth. Net external demand cut 0.6 percentage point, more than the expected 0.4 point drag. Imports jumped as oil and other energy purchases recovered after Japan diversified its supply following disruption from the war in the Middle East. Business investment was the bright spot. It rose 1.6% against a 1.5% forecast, supported by spending on labour-saving technology and AI-related projects. Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said better employment and income conditions, along with policy measures, should support a gradual recovery, but stressed the need to monitor the Middle East situation closely. For the BOJ, which raised rates in June and September, economists say the miss changes little. Several argued that weak consumption is itself a symptom of high prices, which strengthens the case for further hikes, and many expect the next move as soon as December. One note cautioned, however, that if consumer weakness persists, it could widen divisions on the board and give more dovish members grounds to argue for caution. That debate gets an early test later on Monday, when hawkish board member Hajime Takata speaks at 04:00 GMT (11:00 pm ET Sunday). This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: COMAC C919-600 begins flight testing for high-altitude operations in China
articles.desc: China's COMAC has entered the flight testing phase for the C919-600, a shortened variant of its flagship narrow-body aircraft designed specifically for high-altitude operations. This development targets a constrained operational niche within China's domestic network, where thin air limits the usable
articles.content: China's COMAC has entered the flight testing phase for the C919-600, a shortened variant of its flagship narrow-body aircraft designed specifically for high-altitude operations. This development targets a constrained operational niche within China's domestic network, where thin air limits the usable capacity of standard narrow-body jets, effectively reducing the revenue-generating payload on critical routes. The bottleneck in these regions is not a lack of demand, but a physical constraint on thrust and lift. Across China, 46 airports sit above 1,500 meters, with 25 located in "ultra-high-altitude" zones exceeding 2,400 meters. In these environments, standard narrow-body aircraft face significant derating. At Ngari-Gunsa Airport, which sits at 4,274 meters, an Airbus A319 configured for 128 seats is legally limited to carrying no more than 105 passengers to ensure a safe takeoff. This 19% reduction in capacity directly impacts unit cost per seat, making many such flights economically marginal for carriers operating full-weight standard airframes. COMAC's solution for the C919-600 is structural rather than mechanical. By shortening the fuselage by 3.6 meters and removing six frames, the manufacturer reduced the empty weight of the airframe while retaining the standard LEAP-1C engines. According to COMAC, this weight optimization allows the aircraft to carry between 140 and 160 passengers. This represents a substantial increase in usable payload over the derated A319, directly addressing the profitability gap created by high-altitude physics. The variant also includes specific survival and navigation upgrades, including a fourfold increase in passenger oxygen supply duration from 15 to 60 minutes-a critical safety margin in mountainous terrain where diversion to lower altitudes is geographically constrained-and enhanced avionics for navigating narrow valley corridors.

articles.title: U.S. Air Traffic Control Shutdown Caused By Router Data Overload
articles.desc: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy explains how router data overload halted U.S. flights and reveals $12.5 billion spending plan while citing software funding gaps.
articles.content: U.S. Air Traffic Control Shutdown Caused By Router Data Overload | Economy U.S. Air Traffic Control Shutdown Caused By Router Data Overload Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy explains how router data overload halted U.S. flights and reveals $12.5 billion spending plan while citing software funding gaps. U.S. commercial aviation ground to a complete halt on Friday following a critical infrastructure failure within the national confirmed that the disruption was triggered by routers becoming overloaded with data, which caused significant inconsistencies in data transmission across key control centers. The incident forced an emergency nationwide that grounded all domestic flights until operations could be safely resumed the following morning. This event marked one of the most severe disruptions to the American flying public in recent history, affecting thousands of travelers and disrupting supply chains across the nation. Duffy detailed the technical specifics of the failure, explaining that the core issue lay in the routing hardware becoming unable to handle the volume of data flowing through the system. The routers experienced such severe overload that they began returning inconsistent data streams to air traffic controllers and flight operations centers. This technical breakdown rendered the airspace too unstable for safe commercial operations, prompting the decision to issue a comprehensive ground stop to prevent mid-air conflicts and ensure passenger safety during the technical crisis. Air Traffic Control System Failure Grounds US Flights The Secretary clarified that Congress had allocated $12.5 billion specifically for modernization efforts, outlining exactly how those funds were deployed across the agency. The money was directed toward purchasing new radios, installing new radars, implementing electronic flight strips, and upgrading to modern telecom lines. Duffy emphasized that every cent from this allocation has been accounted for and that every piece of physical equipment designated for purchase will be fully installed and operational by the end of 2028, marking a significant milestone in the long-term infrastructure overhaul. Despite the extensive hardware upgrades, Duffy highlighted a critical vulnerability in the current funding structure that left the agency unable to build the core software required to run the modernized system. He stated that Congress had locked the $12.5 billion into physical hardware purchases, effectively leaving the Federal Aviation Administration without the necessary funds to develop the essential software that makes the air traffic control system run efficiently. This disconnect between hardware acquisition and software development has created a systemic risk that threatens the resilience of the entire airspace management network. Operations began slowly returning to normal status on Saturday morning as planes started pushing back from gates, taxiing to runways, and taking off in a phased manner. Duffy assured the public that it is now safe to fly, noting that the agency is in close coordination with major airlines to support the ongoing recovery process. Travelers should expect to continue seeing some delays and cancellations as carriers work to reschedule flights and reposition aircraft and crews where they are needed most to restore the schedule. To avoid a recurrence of this nationwide ground stop, Duffy emphasized that Congress must act as a vital partner in funding the remainder of the modernization build. He argued that the current aging network has been neglected for decades and requires significant investment to ensure it stays resilient for the future. The agency successfully landed over 3,500 planes safely during the crisis, proving that while the physical infrastructure is being upgraded, the software foundation must also be strengthened to handle data loads without failing. Duffy stressed that two realities exist simultaneously: the agency will continue to keep passengers safe

Kurt"CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Cybercriminals are impersonating OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic with fake AI event invitations designed to steal employees’ Microsoft and Google login credentials. Fake AI event invites promise free access to premium tools. After all, plenty of employees want to learn how AI can make their jobs easier. A free premium subscription could be enough to get someone's attention. The phishing pages discovered by Push Security promote events that appear to come from recognizable technology companies. One fake OpenAI event advertised a November 4 livestream called"ChatGPT for Social & Digital Marketing Teams. " The registration page promised three months of ChatGPT Pro to participants. Another page promoted an invitation-only SpaceX briefing scheduled for November 12. Visitors could supposedly choose between three months of Grok Heavy or a"SpaceX share. " Researchers also identified a phishing page impersonating an Anthropic event at AWS re 2026. That page was no longer active when they investigated it. These pages impersonated legitimate technology companies, and the advertised rewards were part of the phishing scheme. Push Security did not suggest that OpenAI, SpaceX or Anthropic operated these fraudulent events. And here's where things get especially concerning. The fake websites tell visitors they must sign in using their corporate Microsoft or Google accounts to complete registration and claim the promised rewards. That request opens the door to the phishing attack. The criminals have put considerable effort into making these invitations appear credible. Rather than sending people directly to an obvious phishing website, they use familiar online services to help disguise where the links lead. Push Security found that the campaign routed visitors through shortened linksand Zapier. Earlier related attacks also used legitimate Zoom event pages and GoTo Webinar's email infrastructure. As a result, someone checking an invitation might see a familiar service before reaching the malicious registration page. Along with Aatmanirbharta, India must be a developer, innovator & global leader in cutting-edge technologies: Defence Minister Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Sunday called for making India not merely a user of advanced technologies, but also a developer, innovator and global leader in critical domains, while stressing that 'Atmanirbharta' (self-reliance) in defence is a "strategic necessity". He also emphasised the need to strengthen the country’s Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) ecosystem to enhance defence preparedness and self-reliance. Virtually addressing the 36th Annual Conference on Non-Destructive Evaluation & Enabling Technologies and the 15th International Symposium on Non-Destructive Testing in Aerospace in Hyderabad, Rajnath Singh stressed the importance of developing indigenous capabilities in advanced inspection technologies, promoting consistent quality assurance practices and ensuring the accuracy, reliability and integrity of testing results, particularly in strategic applications. He asserted that there can be no compromise on the integrity of testing results in strategic applications. "We must strengthen our indigenous capabilities in advanced inspection technologies, specialised sensors, evaluation equipment and associated software. Developing domestic capabilities in these areas is essential for reducing technological dependencies and securing critical defence supply chains," he said, while urging the promotion of consistent quality assurance practices across the entire defence industrial ecosystem. "Public Sector Undertakings, private manufacturers, start-ups and MSMEs have an important role to play in this endeavour. We must ensure that inspection results are accurate, reliable and traceable, and are based on robust procedures and appropriate standards followed by assessment by qualified professionals,” Rajnath Singh added. The Defence Minister stressed that NDT technologies enable examination of the integrity of materials, components and structures without causing any damage to them. Elucidating the concept, he said just as ultrasound and X-rays help examine the human body without surgical intervention, NDT techniques enable the detection of internal defects in critical components without dismantling or damaging them. Highlighting the strategic significance of the sector, the Defence Minister stated that for a country aspiring to achieve technological leadership, the importance of NDT cannot be overstated. "Aatmanirbharta in defence is not merely an economic objective but also a strategic necessity," he asserted. Noting India’s growing indigenous defence ecosystem, Rajnath Singh cited achievements in missile development, naval platforms, aerospace engineering, radar systems and space applications as reflections of the expanding scientific and industrial capabilities of the nation. He described the commissioning of India's first indigenous aircraft carrier, INS Vikrant, as an important milestone in the Aatmanirbhar Bharat journey. He underlined that as Indian defence systems become increasingly sophisticated, every critical material, component, assembly, and manufacturing process must meet the highest standards of quality and reliability. "Hidden defects can affect operational availability, increase maintenance requirements, reduce the service life of equipment and, in critical situations, jeopardise mission success. We need to move beyond a culture of merely identifying defects towards actively preventing them by embedding quality at every stage of the manufacturing process," Rajnath Singh said. articles.content: SpaceX Catches Starship With Giant Mechanical Arms in a Historic First SpaceX achieved a historic milestone on November 14, 2026, when its Starship spacecraft returned from orbit and was caught by giant mechanical arms at its Texas launch facility for the first time. The maneuver marked a major advance toward fully reusable spaceflight, although an explosion involving the rocket’s booster prevented a complete mission success. , where the returning spacecraft approached the launch tower after spending approximately 22 hours in space. Instead of landing on a conventional platform or splashing down in the ocean, Starship descended toward two enormous mechanical arms , the system was designed to catch returning rocket hardware and support rapid reuse between launches. During this mission, the arms successfully secured the spacecraft above the ground, demonstrating a recovery technique that SpaceX hopes will eventually become routine. The maneuver was particularly significant because the company had previously demonstrated tower catches with its , but had never accomplished the same feat with the Starship spacecraft itself. Successfully recovering the upper stage represents another step toward a transportation system in which both major rocket components can return to the launch site and potentially fly again. During its time in space, the vehicle completed , combining operational objectives with a demonstration of new recovery capabilities. These activities made the flight more than an isolated landing experiment. The spacecraft had to complete its orbital mission before returning to the launch site for the demanding final maneuver. Unlike conventional spacecraft recovery systems, which frequently rely on parachutes, ocean landings, or dedicated landing infrastructure, SpaceX’s approach uses the launch tower itself as recovery equipment. In principle, this strategy could reduce the need for heavy landing hardware aboard the spacecraft and allow recovered vehicles to undergo inspections and refurbishment near their launch infrastructure. Whether these advantages translate into shorter turnaround times will depend on future missions, particularly the condition of the recovered spacecraft and the amount of work required before another flight. Reacting to Saturday’s achievement on X, he described the moment as something with implications extending beyond a single spacecraft recovery. “This is actually a bigger deal for humanity than most people can imagine,” Isaacson wrote. He also recalled the engineers’ reactions when Musk insisted that the concept could work. The accomplishment attracted praise from senior U.S. officials, including , who highlighted the significance of the successful maneuver. “It was almost magic,” Isaacman wrote. “Making more believers by the day.” War Secretary Pete Hegseth also congratulated Musk publicly, recognizing the technical accomplishment and its place in American aerospace development. IOWA CITY, Iowa — Iowa City launched a new Affordable Housing Dashboard that gives residents an interactive look at the city's housing landscape. and pulls together information from U.S. Census data, city records, local and national nonprofits and state agencies. City partners, including local and regional housing nonprofits and academic researchers, helped shape it with feedback and data. "The Dashboard brings together information about the City's progress toward its housing goals in one place, making data more accessible and easier for the public to explore," said Nora Cahill, Public Policy Analyst. Housing affordability remains a challenge in Iowa City and communities across the country, according to the city. The tool tracks progress toward the city's housing production goals and actions to improve housing supply, affordability and choice. It also complements the city's Affordable Housing Progress Report and includes frequently asked questions, data sources and additional resources. articles.title: Can a mobile phone really test soil? The technology behind PM Modi's claim explained | VIDEO
articles.desc: PM Modi's remark sparked online jokes, but portable devices that analyse soil and send results to mobile apps already exist.
articles.content: Can a mobile phone really test soil? The technology behind PM Modi's claim explained | VIDEO | Mathrubhumi English PM Modi's remark sparked online jokes, but portable devices that analyse soil and send results to mobile apps already exist. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's remark about testing soil using mobile phones has triggered a wave of jokes and questions online. But can a farmer really put a little soil on a device and get an instant report on its quality and fertiliser requirements? The answer is yes, with an important distinction: the smartphone does not test the soil on its own. It works with a separate, portable testing device that analyses a soil sample and sends the results to a mobile app. Speaking at the Kisan Tak Bharat Agriculture Conference at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on November 12, Modi said arrangements were being developed to enable soil testing through mobile phones. He described a system in which a farmer places a small amount of soil on a mobile-based device and receives a report identifying suitable crops and the type and quantity of fertiliser required. He also referred to sensor-based equipment powered by artificial intelligence (AI), which could provide precise information to farmers at an affordable cost. The remarks soon became a talking point on social media. The Aam Aadmi Party and Cockroach Janta Party shared a clip of the speech along with memes, taking a dig at the Prime Minister. The viral reaction raised a basic question: is this technology real, or is the idea of testing soil through a phone too good to be true? Not by itself. However, portable soil-testing devices that connect to smartphones already exist in India. They use sensors or chemical reactions to examine a small soil sample, while a mobile application displays the results. An India Today report on the science behind Modi's remarks highlighted two examples: NutriSens, a portable testing system developed by Pune-based scientist Dr Rajul Patkar, and Bhu-Parikshak, developed at IIT Kanpur. These devices show that the broader idea of getting soil test results on a phone is not new or imaginary. The phone acts as the interface for the results; the actual analysis is carried out by the testing equipment. How does a mobile-connected soil tester work? One example is NutriSens, which uses a paper-based sensor system to analyse soil. According to NITI Aayog's Frontier Tech Hub, the device can test six soil parameters using just one gram of soil and deliver results through a mobile app in under five minutes. The process involves mixing the soil with a solution that extracts its nutrients. A drop of the prepared liquid is then placed on a disposable paper strip containing tiny sensors. These sensors react to specific substances in the sample and generate electrical signals. A reader interprets those signals and sends the results to the connected phone. The app then displays information about the soil's condition, helping farmers make decisions about fertiliser use. Another approach is used by Bhu-Parikshak, developed by researchers at IIT Kanpur. Instead of relying on chemical reactions, it uses near-infrared light to analyse a soil sample. The device requires around five grams of dry soil. It connects to a smartphone through Bluetooth and generates a soil health report in about 90 seconds. According to IIT Kanpur, the report includes information on parameters such as nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, organic carbon and soil texture, along with fertiliser recommendations. IIT Kanpur announced the launch of Bhu-Parikshak in 2022, saying the device had been made available through an agritech company licensed to distribute it. NutriSens is another example of a portable soil-testing solution already being used by farmers. NITI Aayog's Frontier Tech Hub says NutriSens is being used across eight states and has reached an estimated 10,000 to 15,000 farmers. It also reports that the device can bring down the cost of a soil test from Rs 500 to Rs 30

articles.desc: Explore 7 technologies humans must develop to generate power, extract resources, and survive on a permanent Moon base.
articles.content: NASA's Moon base plans depend on 7 technologies that are still developing - Human Spaceflight | Artemis Program News NASA's Moon base plans depend on 7 technologies that are still developing Explore 7 technologies humans must develop to generate power, extract resources, and survive on a permanent Moon base. A permanent Moon base requires continuous power, local resource extraction, and automated life support. It will also need energy storage systems capable of supplying electricity and heat through extended darkness. NASA is developing a 5G communications system with integrated Wi-Fi 6 to ensure reliable navigation and connectivity near the lunar South Pole. Returning astronauts to the Moon is one challenge. Keeping them there for months or years is another. A permanent lunar base will need much more than a landing vehicle and a pressurized habitat. CSU scientists explore ways to help crops grow with less water and fertilizer It will require reliable power, locally sourced resources, radiation protection, autonomous construction systems, and infrastructure that can survive one of the harshest environments in the solar system. NASA’s plans for a sustained lunar presence near the South Pole highlight how much work remains. The agency is developing technologies for surface power, resource extraction, construction, communications, and dust mitigation, but many still need to be demonstrated and integrated under actual lunar conditions. Here are seven technologies that will be essential to turning the Moon from a destination for short missions into a place where humans can live and work for the long term. Solar panels are an obvious source of electricity on the Moon, but they cannot provide uninterrupted power everywhere. A lunar day and night each last approximately 14 Earth days, and locations in permanent shadow receive little or no direct sunlight.systems capable of supplying electricity and heat through extended darkness, alongside power generation that does not depend on sunlight. NASA is developing vertical solar arrays designed to collect sunlight near the lunar poles, as well as radioisotope power systems and small fission reactors. Nuclear fission could provide a particularly important source of continuous electricity, operating independently of solar conditions. NASA has announced plans forto land on the surface in 2030. However, the reactor and the wider power distribution infrastructure still need to be developed and demonstrated for sustained operations. Transporting every kilogram of water, oxygen, and propellant from Earth would make a permanent settlement extremely expensive. Instead, lunar infrastructure will need to use resources already present on the surface, a process known as in-situ resource utilization . The lunar South Pole is particularly interesting because permanently shadowed craters may contain water ice. If engineers can locate, excavate, and process it at useful scales, the water could support drinking, hygiene, and life-support systems. It could also be separated into hydrogen and oxygen, potentially providing ingredients for rocket propellant. , or regolith, which contains oxygen chemically bound in minerals. NASA researchers demonstrated an integrated solar-carbothermal prototype in 2026 that extracted oxygen from simulated lunar regolith. Scaling such systems for practical surface production remains a major challenge. Astronauts cannot rely on a continuous supply of fresh air and water from Earth. A permanent base will need systems that recycle wastewater, remove carbon dioxide, control humidity, and maintain a breathable atmosphere with minimal human intervention. that recovers approximately 90 percent of its water. It also removes carbon dioxide from cabin air and generates oxygen through water electrolysis. articles.title: Oxford experts secure £520k for new haemophilia treatment trial
articles.desc: The study, led by two specialists from Oxford University Hospitals (OUH), will explore whether a naturally occurring joint fluid could reduce pain.
articles.content: Oxford haemophilia experts secure £520k for clinical trial | Oxford Mail Oxford haemophilia experts secure £520k for clinical trial Pictured, an MRI scan of a haemophilic ankle This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A new clinical trial could improve treatment options for people with haemophilia-related ankle arthritis. The study, led by two specialists from Oxford University Hospitals (OUH), will explore whether a naturally occurring joint fluid could reduce pain and improve mobility for those living with haemophilic arthropathy. Consultant haematologist Dr Nicola Curry and senior haemophilia physiotherapist Steph Taylor have secured £520,000 in funding from the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Research for Patient Benefit programme to conduct the multicentre trial. Dr Curry said: "Steph and I are delighted to have support from the NIHR for this trial. "To be able to deliver this national trial is exciting, as we will be able to provide important answers to our patients. "It has been, and will continue to be, a truly patient-designed clinical trial." The trial will investigate the use of intra-articular hyaluronic acid, sometimes referred to as 'liquid cartilage,' to treat ankle arthropathy in people with haemophilia. A pilot study carried out in 2023 suggested that hyaluronic acid could reduce pain and improve ankle function in these patients. The new funding will support a larger, placebo-controlled trial across the UK. This will allow researchers to determine whether hyaluronic acid can consistently reduce pain, improve joint function, and enhance quality of life for patients with haemophilia. The study has been developed with, and has strong support from, patients with haemophilia.
